h1: 论文英文正文草稿（English Draft）
p: 状态：W3 初稿（2026-10-08），基于统一口径 v1.0 最新实测数字（T2a/T2b/P0/附录 A/R11/R13/QP v1.0 均已收口）。公式与图表编号待与图表蓝图对齐，全部实验数字可在投稿前复核替换。英文正文，供 3 人分工精修。
Set-Valued Intent Understanding with Calibrated Refusal: A Training-Free Retrieval-Grounded Conformal Approach

Web queries are inherently ambiguous: a single utterance can express multiple intents, and long-tail inputs often arrive without context. Entry points that must respond in a single turn—search boxes, instant-messaging assistants, and agent cold starts—therefore need to output an ordered set of intents and, crucially, to decide when to release, clarify, or refuse. Yet existing approaches either rely on multi-turn clarification [6], require vertical-domain grounding [7], or emit generative descriptions without any calibrated refusal guarantee [12].

We propose a training-free framework for single-turn intent understanding that couples multi-intent set output with calibrated refusal. Our method (i) builds a zero-annotation intent knowledge base and applies retrieval-augmented inference to produce a primary intent plus an ordered set of secondary intents; (ii) introduces retrieval-grounded, classifier-free set-valued conformal calibration, which extends conformal prediction from point / fixed-label-set coverage to variable-length multi-intent Jaccard coverage by fusing retrieval statistics with LLM self-assessment—no gradient training is required; and (iii) derives an adaptive minimal clarification set, returning 1 candidate for clear queries, 2–3 for ambiguous ones, and an empty set (refusal) for out-of-scope input.

On CLINC150, MixATIS, and MixSNIPS (two independent runs, \alpha=0.1), the method achieves 100% out-of-scope refusal, expected calibration error as low as 0.005, and tight sets (avg size 0.87 / 1.52 / 1.80) while maintaining the nominal coverage guarantee. It dominates conformal baselines (CICC [31], MULACONF [33], TECP-style [35], UniCR [34]) and the generative set baseline (QP-OneModel [12]) in set compactness and calibration, and under an equal-risk operating point closes the F1 gap to few-shot LLM baselines to ~2.7pt while preserving finite-sample guarantees those baselines do not provide [P0-1].

1.1 The problem. Web queries are inherently ambiguous and composite. The same query can map to multiple intents; users routinely pack several requests into one input; and long-tail queries arrive with little context. Public evidence shows this is a systematic, unsolved gap: TREC CAsT has made ambiguity identification and clarification-question selection a standalone task [15]; on the 663 ambiguous exploratory queries of Needle in the Web, most agents score below 35% accuracy [16]; and the best model on VibeSearchBench reaches only F1 30.30 [8]. Entry points that must respond in a single turn—search boxes, IM assistants, and agent cold starts—have no chance to re-ask. They must return an ordered set of intents in one response and, just as importantly, make a trustworthy decision about whether to release, clarify, or refuse.

1.2 The gap. Existing approaches cover only part of this requirement. Prism [6] decomposes complex intents and drives clarification through an evolving dialogue, but it depends on multi-turn interaction and self-evolving fine-tuning—unavailable in single-turn entries. DoorDash's agentic grounding [7] is effective in its vertical (catalog entities, 90.7% long-tail coverage) but does not generalize to open-web queries. QP-OneModel [12] unifies query understanding under a generative decoder but provides no guaranteed refusal or clarification trigger. Meanwhile, the trustworthiness dimension of intent understanding—out-of-scope (OOS) refusal, confidence calibration, and the cost of false refusal—is under-studied in the Web setting: OOS detectors are notoriously fragile to hard negatives (AUROC drops from 0.964 to 0.810 on Banking77 [20][21]), and calibrated decision-making for open-set intents remains largely unaddressed.

1.3 Our approach and contributions. We propose a training-free framework for single-turn intent understanding that couples multi-intent set output with calibrated refusal. The pipeline is retrieval-grounded: a zero-annotation intent knowledge base (definitions + example utterances, no human labels) is indexed into intent-level prototypes and utterance-level vectors; retrieval-augmented inference feeds the top-K candidates into an LLM, which outputs a primary intent and an ordered set of secondary intents. A calibration module—the core of our method—constructs a fused nonconformity score from retrieval statistics and LLM self-assessment, and performs split conformal calibration on a set-level risk (Jaccard similarity between the predicted set and the true intent set), extending conformal prediction from single-point / fixed-label-set coverage to variable-length multi-intent set coverage without any gradient training. A three-state decision module then returns an adaptive minimal clarification set: 1 candidate for clear queries, 2–3 for ambiguous ones, and 0 (refusal) for out-of-scope input.

Our contributions are four-fold: (1) we present, to our knowledge, the first single-turn framework that unifies multi-intent set output with calibrated refusal, differentiated from multi-turn clarification [6], vertical grounding [7], and guarantee-free generation [12]; (2) we introduce retrieval-grounded, classifier-free set-valued conformal calibration, extending conformal prediction from point / fixed-label coverage to variable-length multi-intent Jaccard coverage; (3) we contribute an adaptive minimal clarification set with three-state decision, calibrated on the validation set under an FPR95 constraint; and (4) we provide an engineering study showing that the training-free route—zero-training deployment, knowledge updatability, accuracy, and calibration—is competitive, with light fine-tuning (LoRA/SetFit) as controlled comparison.

1.4 Results and organization. On CLINC150, MixATIS, and MixSNIPS with two independent runs at α=0.1, our method achieves 100% OOS refusal (CLINC150), ECE 0.005/0.219/0.045, and tight sets (avg 0.87/1.52/1.80). It outperforms conformal baselines (CICC, MULACONF, UniCR) in set compactness and calibration, outperforms the TECP-style entropy baseline in cost (1× vs 5× LLM calls) with comparable calibration, and exceeds the generative QP-OneModel baseline in multi-intent set quality (T2b). Under an equal-risk operating point (P0-1), the F1 gap to the strongest few-shot LLM baseline shrinks to ~2.7pt while our ECE advantage is 6–8×, and the clarify-fair oracle analysis (P0-2) shows our multi-intent gap is largely a reporting-convention difference. Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 formalizes the method; Section 4 details the experimental setup, results, and ablations; Section 5 concludes with limitations and future work.

Our work sits at the intersection of five lines: intent understanding benchmarks, multi-intent and compositional intent, OOS detection and calibration, training-free and efficient intent classification, and Web-scenario intent understanding. Table 3-1 in the design doc summarizes the positioning; below we detail the closest lines.
h3: 2.1 Intent Understanding Benchmarks: From Label Classification to Deeper Capabilities
p: Closed-set benchmarks—CLINC150 (150 intents / 10 domains with native OOS), Banking77, and HWU64—remain the de-facto testbeds [17]. Recent 2025–2026 benchmarks push difficulty further: IntentGrasp unifies intent understanding as multi-choice QA, where 20 frontier models all score below 25% F1 on the hard Gem Set (17/20 below the 15.2% random baseline) while the human baseline is 81.1% [10]; ConsintBench evaluates 20 models on 200k+ real consumer discussions and shows the strongest models still fall short on deep intent understanding [11]. The field is moving from "classify accurately" to "understand deeply and refuse correctly." Our paper follows this trend and makes multi-intent sets plus refusal an evaluable capability dimension.

MixATIS/MixSNIPS first synthesized 1–3-intent mixed queries from ATIS/SNIPS (roughly 3:5:2) [13]; MultiSNIPS further models intent co-occurrence [14]; generative multi-intent detection formulates the task as multi-label output [14]. Existing work focuses on "predict accurately." We bind multi-intent set output to a calibrated refusal decision and, besides Hit@k and intent-set IoU, evaluate when to refuse.

Discriminative OOS baselines remain strong: Mahalanobis distance (AUROC 98.4, FPR95 6.8 on CLINC150) [21]; DROID dual representation (95.88% Unknown on CLINC150) [19]. However, hard-negative OOS sharply degrades AUROC [20], and in multi-party dialogue the F1-OOS is only 45.00 with the human baseline still higher [22]. On the calibration side, temperature scaling and conformal prediction provide candidate sets with coverage guarantees [17]. Our difference: calibration and refusal are wired into a three-state decision and evaluated on decision quality over public ambiguous query sources.

Recent advances in conformal prediction and LLM uncertainty. Conformal prediction (CP) has quickly spread from discriminative classifiers to black-box LLMs. CICC [31] first applied CP to intent classification, constructing calibrated clarification sets with coverage guarantees on a BERT classifier and extending them to OOS—but it is bound to a discriminative backbone and does not handle LLM-native pipelines. UniCR [34] fuses multi-source evidence (self-consistency, retrieval compatibility, etc.) under conformal risk control to enable API-only LLM refusal, yet targets long-form generation with single-label refusal and no intent-set expansion. TECP [35] uses token entropy as a logit-free nonconformity score for prediction sets, again on multi-choice QA. MiRD [36] performs miscoverage risk decomposition on open-domain QA, distinguishing missing vs. wrong answers—conceptually aligned with our stratified loss, but it does not handle primary/secondary intent hierarchy. Xie et al. [37] propose CP for open-set and imbalanced classification; Learnable Conformal Abstention [38] learns thresholds via RL; a survey of CP for NLP appears in [39].

Our positioning. Existing work either binds a discriminative backbone (CICC, Mahalanobis, DROID) or targets single-label choice / long-text QA (UniCR, TECP, MiRD). Ours is the first to apply stratified set-valued conformal to LLM-native multi-intent recognition with dual OOS refusal: a stratified loss explicitly separates main/aux coverage, rank-normalized fusion combines retrieval scores with LLM confidence, and offline split CP provides finite-sample coverage guarantees.

A systematic study of 41 open-weight models shows instruction fine-tuning dominates parameter scale (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct aggregates 0.632, beating most 7B base models), SNIPS is saturated, and calibration effects are inconsistent [18]; hybrid routing (small model + uncertainty → LLM) is the industrial de-facto standard, approaching large-model accuracy at far lower latency [17]. Retrieval-augmented intent classification (REIC) demonstrates the no-retrain advantage [24]; retrieval-based kNN classification is effective in low-resource languages [26]; embedding neighbors are the standard zero-shot text classification route [27]. We therefore adopt a training-free knowledge-base index + retrieval-augmented reasoning + calibrated refusal as our method backbone, with pure-LLM, hybrid routing, and light fine-tuning (LoRA/SetFit) as comparisons.

Prism lowers cognitive load via complex-intent decomposition and a logical clarification sequence [6]; DoorDash serves long-tail queries with catalog-entity retrieval + agentic search + ordered multi-intent sets (90.7% long-tail queries, +13.0pp relative) [7]; QP-OneModel unifies generative query understanding [12]; INTENT-AS-A-TOOL tracks intent signals from the agent-safety side [9]. We differ by not relying on multi-turn interaction or vertical catalogs: we target generic single-turn entries and treat the ordered intent set plus trusted refusal as the minimal deployable loop.
